units.title: Hello, Zig
units.summary: Write your first Zig program, print text and numbers with std.debug.print, and run it with zig run.

lesson.md: A program is a list of instructions for the computer. Zig is a fast language that turns your code into a program before it runs: this step is called **compiling**. This course uses **Zig 0.17**. Here is a complete Zig program:

The first line loads the **standard library**, a collection of ready-made tools, and gives it the name `std`. `pub fn main() void` defines the function `main`: `fn` starts a function, `pub` makes it visible from outside the file, and `void` means it gives back no value. The program starts in `main` and runs the lines between `{` and `}` from top to bottom.

`std.debug.print` shows text. It takes two things: the text in double quotes and a list of values in `.{}`. Here the list is empty. `\n` is a **new line**: `print` does not add one by itself. Every instruction ends with a semicolon `;`.

Inside the text, `{s}` and `{d}` are **placeholders**. Zig replaces them with the values from the list, in order. Use `{s}` for text (a **string**) and `{d}` for a number. Separate the values with commas: `.{ "Ada", 36 }`.
The number of placeholders must match the number of values. If they do not match, or `{d}` gets a string, Zig stops with an error before the program runs. These checks catch many mistakes early.
Save the code in a file that ends with `.zig`, for example `hello.zig`. In a terminal, the command `zig run hello.zig` compiles the file and runs the program right away.

`std.debug.print` writes to the **standard error** stream (stderr), not to the normal output (stdout). In the terminal you see both, so it is perfect for learning. In the exercises, short examples show only the lines inside `main`.

card: `pub fn main() void { }` is where the program starts
`zig run hello.zig` compiles and runs a file

units.title: const, var and types
units.summary: Store values with const and var, meet the types i32, u8, f64 and bool, and see why overflow is an error.

lesson.md: A **variable** is a name for a value. In Zig you create one with `const` or `var`. A `const` value never changes. A `var` value can change later. Use `const` whenever you can.
`var age: i32 = 36` creates a variable `age` of the **type** `i32` with the value `36`. The type comes after the colon `:`. `age += 1` adds 1 to `age`. You can also write `age = age + 1`.

The type says what kind of value a variable holds. `i32` is a whole number that can be negative. `u8` is a whole number from 0 to 255 (`u` means **unsigned**: no minus sign). `f64` is a decimal number. `bool` is `true` or `false`. Print a `bool` with the placeholder `{}`.
With `const name = "Ada"` you do not write a type: Zig works it out from the value. This is called **type inference**. A `var` needs a type when you give it a plain number, as in `var age: i32 = 36`.
You calculate with `+`, `-` and `*`. `%` gives the rest of a division: 26 divided by 7 is 3, rest 5. `-=` and `*=` work like `+=`.
Zig is strict: an unused variable is an error, and so is a `var` that never changes. The compiler then tells you to use `const`.

Every whole-number type has a range. A `u8` holds 0 to 255. `const x: u8 = 256;` does not compile. If a value grows too big while the program runs, the program stops with the message `integer overflow` instead of giving a wrong result.
Here `level` reaches 255, the largest `u8`. With `level += 6` the program would stop with `integer overflow`.

A value that does not fit its type is an error

units.title: Decisions
units.summary: Let your program decide with if and else, combine conditions with and and or, and pick a case with switch.

lesson.md: `if` runs code only when a **condition** is true. The condition goes in parentheses and must be a `bool`. The code after `else` runs when the condition is false.
You compare values with `==` (equal), `!=` (not equal), `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=`. Each comparison gives `true` or `false`. With `else if` you check another condition when the first one is false.
In Zig, `if` can also produce a value. `if (a) x else y` gives `x` when `a` is true and `y` otherwise. Here you need no braces.
Zig combines conditions with words: `a and b` is true when both are true, `a or b` when at least one is true. `!a` turns `true` into `false` and back.

lesson.output:

You are under 18

lesson.md: `switch` compares one value with several cases. Each case has the form `value => result`. You can list several values with commas or a range like `3...5` (three dots, both ends included). A `switch` must cover every possible value, so you usually end with `else`.
Like `if`, `switch` gives a value. That is why the whole `switch` ends with `};`.

units.title: Loops
units.summary: Repeat code with while and for, count over ranges like 0..5, go through lists, and use break and continue.

lesson.md: A **loop** repeats code. `while` repeats as long as its condition is true. The counter must be a `var`, because it changes in every round.
You can put the step into the loop head: `while (i < 5) : (i += 1)`. The part after the colon runs at the end of every round.
If the condition of a `while` never becomes false, the loop runs forever. Make sure the counter changes.
`for (0..3) |i|` runs once for each number from 0 up to 3, **without** 3: 0, 1 and 2. The name between the bars `|i|` holds the current number. Its type is `usize`, an unsigned whole number.

lesson.output:
1 squared is 1
2 squared is 4
3 squared is 9

lesson.md: `for` also goes through a list of values. `[_]u32{ 3, 5, 8 }` is such a list, called an **array**. You learn more about arrays in a later unit. `for (prices) |p|` gives you each value in turn.
`continue` skips the rest of the current round and goes to the next one. `break` ends the loop at once.
When an `if` controls only one instruction, you can write it on one line without braces, as in `if (i > 7) break;`.

units.title: Functions
units.summary: Write your own functions with parameters and return types, use their results, and solve problems with recursion.

lesson.md: A **function** gives a piece of code a name, so you can use it many times. You already know `main`. You define your own functions with `fn`, outside of `main`, and call them by name.

`name: []const u8` is a **parameter**: a name and its type. `[]const u8` is the type for text; a later unit explains it. The type after the parentheses is the **return type**. `void` means the function gives back nothing.
To give back a value, write its type after the parentheses and use `return`. Separate several parameters with commas.
Parameters are constants: you cannot change them inside the function. Zig also refuses unused parameters, and a result you do not use. To throw a result away on purpose, write `_ = add(1, 2);`.
`return` ends the function at once. That is why `max` needs no `else`. A function can return any type, for example a `bool`.
A function can call itself. This is called **recursion**. It needs a **base case** that stops the calls, otherwise they never end. The factorial of 4 is 4 * 3 * 2 * 1.
The order of functions in a file does not matter. You can write `factorial` below `main` and still call it.

card: `fn add(a: i32, b: i32) i32 { return a + b; }`
Parameters are constants and must be used
Recursion: a function calls itself, with a base case

units.title: Arrays and slices
units.summary: Keep many values in arrays, look at parts of them with slices, and work with text as []const u8.

lesson.md: An **array** holds a fixed number of values of the same type. `[3]i32` is an array of three `i32` values. With `[_]` Zig counts the values for you. You read a value by its **index** in square brackets. The first index is 0. `.len` gives the number of values.
In a `var` array you can change the values. The length stays the same.
An index must be smaller than `.len`. `nums[3]` on an array with three values is an error: the program does not compile, or it stops with `index out of bounds`.

A **slice** is a view of a part of an array. `nums[1..3]` contains the values at index 1 and 2: like a range, the end is not included. A slice also has `.len`. A function that takes a slice such as `[]const u32` works with arrays of any length. You pass a whole array with `&prices`.

Text is a list of bytes. A string is usually a slice of `u8`: `[]const u8`. Each byte is a number. `'h'` in single quotes is one character, which is also a `u8`. Print a whole string with `{s}` and one character with `{c}`. You cannot compare two strings with `==`: use `std.mem.eql(u8, a, b)`, which is `true` when both have the same bytes.
`for (names, 0..) |name, i|` goes through the array and counts at the same time: `name` is the value and `i` its index. `[_][]const u8` is an array of strings.

card: Text is `[]const u8`; compare with `std.mem.eql(u8, x, y)`

units.title: Structs
units.summary: Group values into your own types with struct, give fields default values, and add methods that use self.

lesson.md: A **struct** groups several values into one new type. Each value is a **field** with a name and a type. You create a value with `Point{ .x = 3, .y = 4 }` and read a field with a dot: `p.x`.
Struct names start with a capital letter, like `Point`. In a `var` you can change the fields.
A field can have a **default value**: `level: u32 = 1`. When you create the struct, you can leave this field out. All other fields must be set.
A function inside a struct is a **method**. Its first parameter, usually called `self`, is the value you call it on. You write `r.area()`, and Zig passes `r` as `self`.
`self` is a constant. To change fields, the method takes `self: *Counter`. The star `*` makes it a **pointer**: the method works on the original value. You can call such a method only on a `var`.
Now you know what `.{ name, age }` in `std.debug.print` is: a struct without a type name that holds the values in order.

card: `const Point = struct { x: i32, y: i32 };`
`fn area(self: Rect) u32` is a method: `r.area()`

units.title: Errors and optionals
units.summary: Handle things that can fail with error sets, !T, try and catch, and values that can be missing with ?T and orelse.

lesson.md: Some operations can fail. In Zig an **error** is a value. An **error set** lists the possible errors: `error{ Negative, TooOld }`. A function that can fail has a return type like `AgeError!i32`: the result is an `i32` **or** an error. `return AgeError.TooOld;` returns an error.

You cannot use the result directly: you must handle the error first. `catch 0` means: use `0` if there is an error. With `catch |err|` you get the error itself and can react to it. `{}` prints an error.
Here the return type is only `!u32`, and the error is written as `error.Odd`. Zig then collects the error set by itself. The `return` inside the `catch` block ends `main`.

`try` is a short form: `try half(8)` gives the value, or returns the error to the caller at once. A function that uses `try` must have a `!` in its return type. Also `main` can be `pub fn main() !void`. If an error leaves `main`, the program stops and shows the error.
Sometimes a value is missing. The type `?usize` is a `usize` **or** `null`, which means no value. `orelse` gives a fallback value for `null`.
`if (opt) |v|` runs the block only when there is a value, and `v` holds it. The `else` block runs for `null`.
Use `catch` for errors and `orelse` for optionals. An error tells you **why** something failed. `null` only says that there is no value.

card: `const E = error{ A, B };` and `fn f() E!u32`
`!u32` is a `u32` or an error; `try` passes the error on
